claim: The spec's status is "grilled", in rounds 1 and 2 on 2026-10-23.
The spec was approved on 2026-10-23 at Gate 1.
The decision record for this spec is ADR 0004 (browser search).
Choices the user made are quoted or marked "(user)"; everything marked "(my call)" was decided by Claude and is open to change.
The user likes web-mcp but not its search.
Running SearXNG in Docker on every machine is annoying, and when SearXNG isn't running, `search` fails outright.
On 2026-10-22 both test searches on this machine answered "SearXNG is not reachable".
The user said the results could be "drastically improved".
Today SearXNG scrapes Bing and Yahoo, which serve one index.
Today web-mcp throws away the engines' rank and snippets and ranks passages against the whole archive.
The user rejected every keyed or hosted option and Claude's own WebSearch: paid APIs "cost money", free ones "dont allow scraping", and a scraper "is the same problem like searxng".
The user wants a "claude browser" where Claude queries, with complete isolation, doesn't mind a window opening briefly as long as results are good, and wants to be a "normal" user.
`search` opens the search engines' own result pages in a browser that belongs to web-mcp, reads them like a person would, and builds its answer from that.
Slower is fine: the user accepted 3–5 s per search ("I rather be bit slower and lose all the headache with the limitations etc").
Goal 1: no SearXNG, no keys, no Docker.
`search` must work on any machine where the installer set up agent-browser and its Chrome; `browser` and the fetch fallback already do today.
SearXNG goes away completely, including the installer's Docker step (user: "searxng goes away completly!").
(my call, from "completely") Removing SearXNG does not depend on the bench: if a threshold misses, the browser search is tuned; SearXNG is not kept as a fallback.
Goal 2: each web search opens the result pages of several engines in parallel in web-mcp's own browser.
The search reads each result's URL, title and snippet off the rendered page.
The web engines are Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo and Brave, all opened in parallel on every search (grill Q1, user: "these four should be alright").
No engine that only resells another engine's results is used (user: "We dont need engines that just use another engine"), so Startpage and Yahoo are out.
DuckDuckGo stays even though its links are largely sourced from Bing, because it has its own crawler (grill Q11, user: "has its own crawler stay").
Goal 3, isolation, is the user's requirement.

The browser has a persistent profile of its own kept by web-mcp; it is never the user's Chrome, profile, cookies or Google account and is never attached to it (`--auto-connect` and `--cdp` are not used).
(my call) The profile is persistent so it keeps cookies and consent choices like a normal user's browser.
There is one profile per engine, per user and machine, not per project (plan review round 1, D1, user: "then lets go with A").
Reason for one profile per engine: Chrome can't open one profile twice, the engines run in parallel, and one Chrome can't be headless for some engines and headed for others.
Each engine's Chrome stays open for about 2 minutes after its last search, then closes itself.
Searches that arrive while an engine's Chrome is busy wait their turn per engine instead of failing.
On Windows, each engine's Chrome closes right after its search instead of staying warm (plan review round 2, user: "A").
Reason for closing on Windows: there agent-browser shows browsers with extensions on the visible desktop, so a warm one would linger as a window.
The search browser starts with every `AGENT_BROWSER_*` environment variable removed and in its own folder (plan review round 1, D4: yes).
Neither the user's agent-browser settings nor a project's `agent-browser.json` can attach the search browser to the user's Chrome or change its profile.
(my call, after the builder check) Only `search` uses the persistent profile; the `browser` tool and the fetch fallback keep their throwaway sessions.
Reason: otherwise a page Claude opens, prompt-injected ones included, could set cookies or change consent in the profile every later search uses.
agent-browser 0.39.1 (checked in its README at v0.39.1) has `--profile <path>` (persistent custom profile directory), `--headed`, `--user-agent` and `tab new`.
Goal 4: a normal user with no chores: no CAPTCHA solving, no prompts, nothing the user has to click.
A window may open briefly (user).
Consent banners are handled by an extension, not by web-mcp's own code (user: "could we install extensions that do it automaticly?").
The extension is Consent-O-Matic, from Aarhus University, MIT licensed.

Consent-O-Matic's README says it answers more than 200 CMPs; its `rules/` folder has `bing.json` and five Google rules (`google_consentdomain_1/2`, `google_cwiz`, `google_eomdialog`, `google_popup`), checked 2026-10-23.
The extension is loaded with agent-browser's `--extension <path>`, which works headless and headed (0.39.1 README).
The search profile is declared in one config file (grill Q12, user: "is there no way to just say profile has x extensions?").
Chrome has no per-profile extension list short of admin policies (root or the registry).
agent-browser's config file takes every flag as a camelCase key, so it can name the profile directory, the extensions, the `executablePath`, the user agent and `headed`.
web-mcp keeps one config file beside the search profile and passes it with `--config` on every call to a search session.
A call without `--config` relaunches agent-browser's default browser and the page is lost (spike, D-1).
`--config` replaces `~/.agent-browser/config.json` and a project `agent-browser.json` (findings.md).
Search calls still run with the search folder as working directory.
`args` holds no commas, because agent-browser splits it on commas and newlines.
On Linux, `executablePath` for Helium is a small `#!/bin/sh` wrapper that web-mcp writes beside the profile, running Helium without `exec`.
Reason for the Helium wrapper: nixpkgs' Helium otherwise dies 10 s after agent-browser starts it (findings.md, upstream #1157).
web-mcp itself downloads the pinned Consent-O-Matic Chromium release zip (v1.1.5 today) on the first search, checks its sha256 and unpacks it into the search profile's folder.
The installer has no step for downloading the extension (grill Q12: yes).

The browser is set as `executablePath` and is never the user's installed branded Chrome, because since Chrome 137 branded Chrome ignores extensions loaded from a folder (Chromium PSA) (grill Q12: yes).

Browser order (D-1, user: "there is helium", "let's continue"): `WEB_MCP_CHROME`; else the newest Chrome for Testing from `agent-browser install` if it starts (`--version`, checked once per process; it doesn't on NixOS); else `helium`, then `chromium` on PATH.
When no browser is found, the search fails with a message naming `WEB_MCP_CHROME`.
Consent-O-Matic is not loaded for Bing: with it, Bing's result page dies (spike, D-1).
`open` reporting success proves nothing (it succeeds for a blank page); an engine's outcome comes only from parsing its page.
(my call) Consent-O-Matic's choices are "reject" for everything.
(left to the builder, check first) How Consent-O-Matic's preferences are preset without the onboarding page it shows on install.

(my call, after the builder check) "Normal browser" settings are allowed: a regular Chrome user agent (headless Chrome otherwise announces itself as `HeadlessChrome`), a real window size and `Accept-Language`; anything beyond that is the stealth anti-goal.
Headless or headed is a fixed setting per engine, not a runtime retry (grill Q2, user: "lets first try headless during implementation. The engines that fail get no headless the rest stays headless").
Every engine starts headless; one that is blocked headless during implementation is switched to headed for good, and the plan records which.
Goal 5: one engine failing never fails the search.
"Blocked" means a CAPTCHA or "unusual traffic" page, or a consent wall that doesn't clear; only blocked earns the rest (plan review round 1, D3: yes).
An engine's own "no results" page is an empty answer, not a block.
A network error, a timeout or an unrecognised page skips that engine for this search only, with no rest.
A blocked engine is skipped and rests for 30 minutes.
The rest is shared by every web-mcp process on the machine (grill Q3: yes).
The answer's source line names the engines used and the ones skipped, each with its reason.
Only when every engine fails does `search` fail, and its error names each engine's reason.
Goal 6, better ranking, has its prior art in flow.md#prior-art.
Fusion: the engines' lists are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, and URLs are normalised before merging.
Snippets as evidence: each result's snippet is a passage of this search, like a fetched page's passages.
FreshPrompt found that more snippets meant better answers.
Fetching: the top pages by fused rank are fetched, as today; (my call) the default count stays 5 and the bench may raise it.
Scope: passages are ranked only among this search's snippets and pages; archived passages from earlier searches are no longer ranked at all, but the archive is still written (grill Q4: yes).
The persistent passage index (`.web/index/`) is no longer written since nothing reads it; an existing one stays on disk untouched (plan review round 1, D2: A).
The final order combines BM25 with the fused engine rank (my call); the exact formula is left to the builder and tuned on the bench.
Goal 7: scholarly engines go through the browser (user: "we dont need an api. We have the browser").
`papers: true` also opens Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar result pages.
(my call, offered to the user) OpenAlex, arXiv and Crossref stay as APIs, for clean DOI, abstract and PDF data.
Paper results are merged by DOI or arXiv id, as `papers::merge` does today, then by normalised title.
Scholar and Semantic Scholar follow the same block-and-rest rule as the web engines.
Goal 8, filters without SearXNG, is my call.
`since` (day, week, month, year) maps to each engine's own date filter; an engine without one is skipped for that search and named.
`engines` picks which engines to open, from `google`, `bing`, `duckduckgo`, `brave`, `scholar`, `semanticscholar`; an unknown name is refused with the known list.

(my call, after the builder check) Engines belong to a mode: `scholar` and `semanticscholar` are valid only with `papers: true`, web engines only without it; a mismatch is refused with the mode's list.
`since` applies to both the engines' date filters and OpenAlex's and arXiv's publication-date filters.
Crossref is asked only for DOI lookups, as today, so `since` doesn't reach it (plan review round 2, user: "A").
`category` is removed; site-scoped searches use `site:` in the query, which every engine understands, and the tool description says so.
Goal 9, measured not claimed, is my call; the user's first web-mcp round was benchmark-driven.
A search-quality bench runs a fixed query set through the new search, and through the new search limited to `engines: bing` as the baseline.
There is no SearXNG run in the bench; the user said "we dont need that. As long as SearXNG is gone its alright. After all just using bing should be the same".
(my call) The bing-only run stands in for today's Bing+Yahoo.
The query set is about 30 queries covering coding and docs, general web and fresh facts, and papers, each with a labelled answer or expected source.
The bench reports answer recall: the share of queries whose returned passages contain the labelled answer.
The bench reports per-engine block rate.
The bench reports p50 and p95 latency.
Thresholds are set at Gate 1.
Goal 10: the built-in WebSearch and WebFetch are denied once web-mcp's browser works, not once SearXNG answers.
"Works" means agent-browser is present and `agent-browser install` succeeded.
Every SearXNG mention is removed from the shipped code and docs: README, plugin and marketplace `description`s, `.mcp.json`, tool descriptions, GLOSSARY, CLAUDE.md.
Earlier flows' docs stay as history and keep their SearXNG mentions.
The thresholds were fixed in the grill.
Q1 (quality): answer recall of the new `search` is at least 0.10 above its own bing-only run, and at least 0.70 absolute.
Q2 (speed): p50 at most 5 s, p95 at most 10 s.
Q3 (reliability): at least one web engine answers on at least 95% of queries.
Q3 (reliability): no engine's block rate is above 20% over a run of the whole set, with the profile already warm.
Any API key, paid API or hosted search API for any source is a non-goal; the three existing paper APIs stay.
Claude Code's built-in WebSearch as a backend is a non-goal.
SearXNG in any form, local or remote, is a non-goal.
macOS or ARM support is a non-goal.
Automatic CAPTCHA solving or captcha services are a non-goal.
It is a failure if the user has to click, solve or confirm anything during a search.
It is a failure if web-mcp touches the user's own Chrome, profile or accounts.
It is a failure if one blocked engine makes `search` fail or hang past its deadline.

Stealth plugins, injected scripts that patch browser fingerprints (such as `navigator.webdriver`) and rotating identities to hide the automation are failures: the point is to be a normal browser, not a disguised bot (my call, from "just want to be a normal user").
The installer stops setting up SearXNG and leaves an existing `searxng` container and its `settings.yml` alone; there is no cleanup step (grill Q5, user: "no - I havent really installed it on many").
The installer denies the built-in WebSearch and WebFetch once agent-browser is present and `agent-browser install` succeeded; if that fails they stay allowed (grill Q6: yes).
Claude writes the ~30 queries with their labelled answers; the user skims them once before the first run, then they are fixed (grill Q8: yes).
Thresholds Q1–Q3 as proposed are fixed (grill Q9: yes).
The `search` tool keeps its name and its `query`, `papers` and `max_passages` parameters.
`engines` and `since` work as in goal 8 and `category` is removed.
No new tools are added (grill Q10: yes).
The locale is English, fixed, for every engine (Google `hl=en`, and each engine's own equivalent) (user: "english pls").
The locale doesn't depend on the machine's locale or IP region.
A query written in German still finds German pages.
The work is in the Rust crate `crates/web-mcp`, with agent-browser pinned at 0.39.1 in `installer/assets/agent-browser.json`.
agent-browser is driven as a child process (`browser.rs`, one `--json` call or batch per action).
The targets are Windows and Linux x64.
The engine parsers are parsers of what other tools write and test against captured result pages in fixtures (CLAUDE.md's rule), not assumed shapes.
Everything pulled lands in `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.web/` before Claude sees it, including each engine's result listing, as today's search listing is archived.
Page content stays marked untrusted.
Installer changes use Node's standard library only, with new logic in `core/` or `system/` and a test next to it.
Several web-mcp processes may run at once, one per Claude session, and agent-browser sessions are global per user (`browser.rs:236`).
The per-engine result URLs and parsers, block detection, deadlines, the rest period and the headed retry are left to the builder.
The fusion and the final scoring formula are left to the builder, tuned on the bench.
How Consent-O-Matic's preferences are preset, and where `agent-browser install` puts Chrome for Testing on each OS, are left to the builder.
